title: Reserve commit pattern clustering and simulation notes
body:
Purpose / context:
- Quick working notes for an experiment that clusters customer commit shapes and runs micro-simulations to estimate realistic utilization tail risk and burst budget needs for reserved GPU pools. Goal is to inform 1) tiered commit pricing bands, 2) recommended burst buffer sizing, 3) contract language for phasing and early-exit credits.

Key questions we're trying to answer (working):
1) If we group customers by commit pattern (steady, diurnal, spiky, onboarding-wave), what percent of total reserved capacity is latent (idle) vs volatilily-required?
2) How much burst capacity (as a percent of committed pool) is needed to keep 99th percentile latency SLO without requiring degraded models?
3) What's the breakeven blended rate if we price burst at 2.5x vs 4x on-demand credit?
4) For committed pools, how many days of lookback and what smoothing windows produce the best predictor for next-quarter utilization?

Dataset and inputs used (notes on sources):
- Historical 18 months of pool-level utilization traces (aggregated token/sec and active-job-count) from prod-dedicated (anonymized customer IDs). Data resolution: 5m buckets.
- Customer metadata: committed GPU count, region, SLA tier, contract start date, onboarding wave markers.
- Off-peak reclaim policy traces: how often we reassign slack to short-term backfill in last 12 months.
- Assumptions: quantization/packing improvements reduce average GPU-hours by 8% on steady inference loads; ignore model-variant routing for first pass.

Clustering approach (experiment 1):
- Feature engineering: for each customer-quarter window build a feature vector: mean utilization fraction, std dev, skewness, fraction of 5m buckets > 80% of commit, max consecutive hours above 80%, diurnal amplitude (peak - trough normalized), onboarding indicator.
- Algorithm: MiniBatch KMeans (k from 4..12) with silhouette validation + manual interpretability check. Also a quick HDBSCAN run to find noise/outlier spike customers.
- Outcome (observed clusters):
  * Cluster A - Steady low (40-60% mean, low std): long-lived background traffic, good for packing suggestions.
  * Cluster B - Diurnal enterprise (50-85% with strong daily amplitude): predictable peak windows.
  * Cluster C - Spiky startup / bursty (low mean, high skew): high risk for bursts and latency SLO violations.
  * Cluster D - Onboarding waves (high early-quarter variance): usually ramping up after contract start.
  * Outliers: one-off demos/benchmarks - candidate for special short-term offers.

Micro-simulation design (experiment 2):
- Simulator primitives: per-customer synthetic day generator (sample from historical bucket distribution conditioned on cluster), job arrival model (Poisson for steady, bursty compound Poisson for spiky), backfill policy (best-effort reclaim with preemption cost), and burst purchase decision (on-demand credits pulled from shared pool).
- Pool-level rules: prioritization: committed traffic > burst credits > best-effort backfill. Backfill is allowed only if reserved pool utilization < 70% for 30 consecutive minutes.
- Pricing knobs: burst_price_multiplier in {2.0, 2.5, 3.5, 4.0}, burst_pool_size as % of committed GPUs in {5,10,20,30}.
- Metrics collected per run: 95/99/99.9 percentile token latency, percent requests served from committed capacity, burst cost as percent of total revenue, idle_gpu_hours, frequency of preemption events.

Preliminary simulation results (high-level):
- For a 1000-GPU committed aggregate with realistic customer mix observed, moving from no-burst to 10% burst_pool reduces 99th token latency violations by ~45% for bursty cluster loads, at an incremental cost of ~3.8% of committed revenue when burst_price_multiplier=3.5.
- Increasing burst size beyond 20% shows diminishing returns for 99.9th percentile (tail driven by rare multi-customer simultaneous spikes).
- Pricing sensitivity: low multiplier (2.0) leads to burst being used too often; cost neutrality requires multiplier >=3.0 when burst pool is uncapped for a heterogenous mix.

Heuristics drafted for product/pricing team (candidate recommendations):
1) Default burst buffer: 10% of committed pool for mid-tier contracts, 5% for single-tenant high-commit enterprise, 15% for PLG startups with known spike patterns.
2) Burst pricing: recommend tiered multipliers: 2.5x for first 10% of burst usage/month, 3.5x beyond that. This incentivizes modest bursting while protecting economics.
3) Phased commit clauses: allow customers to increase committed capacity within quarter with pro-rated pricing; for early downsizes within first 90 days charge a 15% smoothing fee unless replaced by a new committed customer in same region.
4) Onboarding credit: offer one-time 200 GPU-hour onboarding credit at 0.0x multiplier to reduce friction for wave customers; track conversions to sustained commit within 60 days.
5) Pack-and-quant recommendations: for Cluster A customers propose auto-pack schedule nightly; expected uplift to utilization by 6-10% (conservative).

Edge cases / risks / follow-ups:
- Correlated spikes (e.g., multiple customers doing simultaneous model evaluation after a public event) drive tail risk much higher than single-customer simulation. We need event correlation modeling (paper: "Modeling Extremal Dependence in Demand" for reference).
- Outlier detection needs operational integration into onboarding (flagging customers as "demo/benchmark" so we do not treat them as normal commit).
- Legal/contract: decide whether burst pricing is invoiced monthly as a separate line item or reconciled into overage credit buckets. Billing flow impacts churn perception.

Short experiment to run next (tactical):
1) Re-run clustering restricting to last 6 months to capture seasonality change post-quantization rollout.
2) Add correlated-event synthetic traces: create a stress test day where 8% of customers in region simultaneously trigger a 6x traffic burst; measure tail.
3) Produce a 1-page customer-facing note (for AE) explaining burst buffer & pricing rationale with a small illustrative example.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Clean PR for capacity-sim to expose per-customer percentiles (Marcus).
- Ask legal for sample contract language templates for phased commit and onboarding-credit (Priya).
- Validate simulation config with SRE team: confirm backfill preemption semantics match runtime behavior (Omar).

Appendix: quick pseudo "spreadsheet" excerpt (columns as plaintext)
- cols: customer_id | cluster | commit_gpus | mean_util% | 95p_util% | peak_hours_above_80% | burst_usage_est_10%pool | suggested_commit_trim
- row1: CUST-001 | Steady | 80 | 52 | 78 | 2 | 3 GPU-hrs/day | 0
- row2: CUST-234 | Spiky | 24 | 18 | 92 | 30 | 12 GPU-hrs/day | recommend convert 4 GPUs to burst-capable
- row3: CUST-987 | Onboard | 200 | 36 | 96 | 120 | 40 GPU-hrs/day | monitor first quarter

End.
